To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
atypical substitutions in Kv6 S6 restrict heteromeric Kv2:K6 stoichiometry to a 3:1 ratio.
atypical substitutions in S6 gates of regulatory Kv subunits limit stoichiometry of functional heteromeric channels to 3:2R.
atypical substitutions in S6 gate sequence distinguish “Regulatory” Kv subunit, which cannot homomerize due to T‐1 self‐incompatability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that control the assembly and function of heteromeric voltage‐gated potassium (Kv) channels.
the molecular mechanisms of voltage‐gating in ion channels.
the evolution of voltage-gated potassium channels (Kv channels) in the nervous system, with a particular focus on the Kv6 family of regulatory channels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Kv6.4 is a self-incompatible subunit and that its self-incompatibility and the atypical S6 gate are both necessary for the formation of Kv2.
Kv6 subunits are not self‐compatible, and that the atypical S6 substitutions are responsible for restricting the stoichiometry.
Kv6.4 and Kv8.3 are the only Kv6 and Kv8 subunits, respectively, that have been shown to form heteromeric channels with Kv2.2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the S6 activation gates of the regulatory subunits are not only responsible for their regulatory phenotype but also for their stoichiometry.
Kv6 subunits are not only self‐incompatible with Kv6 subunits, but also self‐incompatible within Kv2 subunits.

the Kv subfamily has undergone a long evolutionary history of subfamily‐specific specialization, with each subfamily acquiring a unique set of functions and properties that are critical for neuronal function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stoichiometry is restricted by a combination of T1 self‐ incompatibility and S6 gate sequence.
Kv6 and Kv8 subunits are not just regulatory, but also have a functional role.
the S6 activation gates of Kv subunits have evolved to be compatible with the T1 domain of their cognate subfamily, and that this compatibility is necessary for homotetrameric channel function.
